translations.text: King David was old and advanced in years. They covered him with clothes, but he could not get warm.

His servants said to him, “Here are your servants before you. Let them look for a young virgin for our lord the king. Let her stand before the king and be his attendant, and let her lie in your arms so that our lord the king may get warm.”
They searched for a beautiful young woman throughout the territory of Israel. They found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very beautiful. She became the king’s attendant and served him, but the king did not have sexual relations with her.
Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king.” He provided himself with chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him.
His father had never rebuked him by saying, “Why are you doing this?” He too was very handsome, and his mother had borne him after Absalom.
He held discussions with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they supported Adonijah.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Dai, and David’s mighty warriors did not follow Adonijah.

Adonijah sacrificed sheep, cattle, and fattened animals at the great stone beside the Fuller’s Spring. He invited all his brothers, the king’s sons, everyone from the house of Judah, and the king’s servants.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, David’s mighty warriors, or his brother Solomon.
Nathan the prophet said to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, “Have you not heard that Adonijah has become king, and our lord David does not know?
Now come, let me give you advice, and save your life and the life of your son Solomon.

Go in to King David and say to him, ‘Did you not, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, “Your son Solomon will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne”? Why, then, has Adonijah become king?’
While you are still speaking there before the king, I will come in after you and confirm your words.”
Bathsheba went in to King David in his bedroom. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.
Bathsheba knelt and bowed before the king. The king said to her, “What is it, Bathsheba?”
She said to him, “My lord the king, you swore by the LORD your God to your servant, saying, ‘Your son Solomon will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne.’
But now Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, do not know.

He has sacrificed cattle, fattened animals, and many sheep. He invited all the king’s sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
As for you, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, waiting for you to tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
When my lord the king rests peacefully with his ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals.”
While she was still speaking there before the king, Nathan the prophet arrived.
They informed the king, saying to him, “Nathan the prophet has arrived.” He came in before the king, fell facedown to the ground, and bowed.
Nathan said, “My lord the king, did you say, ‘Adonijah will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne’?

For Adonijah has gone down today and sacrificed cattle, fattened animals, and many sheep. He has invited all the king’s sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. They are now eating and drinking before him and saying, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’
But he did not invite me, your servant, or Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
Has this matter come from you, my lord the king, without your telling your servants who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?
King David answered, “Call Bathsheba to me.” She came in before him and stood before the king.
The king swore to her, saying, “As the LORD lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble,
just as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, ‘Your son Solomon will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne,’ so I will do today.”
Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground, paid homage to the king, and said, “May my lord King David live forever!”
King David said, “Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada to me.” They came before the king.
The king said to them, “Get up, take your lord’s servants with you, have my son Solomon ride on my own mule, and lead him down to Siloam.
There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him to reign over Israel. Blow the trumpet and say, ‘Long live King Solomon!’”
Go up after him, and let him come and sit on my throne. He will reign after me. I have appointed him to be king over Israel and Judah.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king, “Amen! May the LORD your God do so.
Just as the LORD has been with my lord the king, so may he also be with Solomon, and may he make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David.”
Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the archers, and the slingers went down. They had Solomon ride on King David’s mule and led him to Siloam.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. They blew the trumpet, and all the people said, “Long live King Solomon!”
All the people went up after him, playing flutes and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth split with their noise.
Adonijah and all his invited guests heard it as they finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, “What is this noise? Why is the city in an uproar?”
While he was still speaking, Nathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said to him, “Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news.”
Nathan answered Adonijah, “Indeed, our lord King David has made Solomon king.
The king sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the archers, and the slingers with him, and they had Solomon ride on the king’s mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him king there at Siloam. They came up from there rejoicing, and the whole city rejoiced. That is the noise you heard.
Solomon has also taken his seat on the royal throne.

The king’s servants also came to bless our lord King David, saying, ‘May the LORD your God make Solomon’s name more renowned than yours and his throne greater than your throne.’ The king bowed down on his bed.
The king also said, ‘Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, who today has given me a son to sit on my throne while my own eyes see it.’”
All the men who were Adonijah’s invited guests became afraid. They got up and went away, each on his own way.
Adonijah was afraid of Solomon, so he got up, went away, and took refuge by grasping the horns of the altar.

King Solomon was told, “Adonijah is afraid of you and has taken refuge by grasping the horns of the altar. He says, ‘Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not kill his servant with the sword.’”
Solomon said, “If he proves to be a worthy man, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground. But if evil is found in him, he will die.”
King Solomon sent for him and had him brought from the altar. He came and bowed down to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, “Go home.”
When the time drew near for David to die, he gave instructions to his son Solomon, saying to him:
“I am going the way of all the earth. Be strong and be a man.

Keep the requirements of the Lord your God, walk in his ways, and keep his statutes, commandments, judgments, and testimonies, as written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in everything you do and succeed wherever you go.

Then the Lord will fulfill the words he spoke concerning me: ‘If your sons guard their ways, walking before me faithfully with all their heart and all their soul, you will never lack a man to sit on the throne of Israel.’

Now you know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, and what he did to the two commanders of Israel’s armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them, treating them as though they were in battle. He shed their blood with the sword at his waist and trampled it with the sandals on his feet.
Deal with him according to your wisdom, and do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace.
But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, because they provided for me in everything when I fled from your brother Absalom.

And here with you is Shimei son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin, from Bahurim. He cursed me bitterly on the day I went to Mahanaim. But he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the Lord God, saying, ‘I will not kill you with the sword.’
Now do not let him go unpunished, for you are a wise man and know what to do to him. Bring his folly back upon his own head, and bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood.”
David slept with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David.
David reigned over Israel for forty years. He reigned in Hebron for seven years, and in Jerusalem for thirty-three years.
Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.
Adonijah son of Haggith came to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother. She said to him, “Do you come in peace?” He said, “In peace.”
He said to her, “I have something to say to you.” She said to him, “Speak.”

He said to her, “You know that the kingdom rightfully belonged to me, and that all Israel looked to me to become king. But the kingdom was taken from me and became my brother’s, because it came to him from the Lord.
Now I have one request to make of you. Do not refuse me.” She said to him, “Speak.”
He said to her, “Speak to King Solomon, for he will not refuse you, and ask him to give me Abishag the Shilomite as my wife.”
Bathsheba said, “Very well. I will speak to the king on your behalf.”

Bathsheba went in to King Solomon to speak to him about Adonijah. The king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne, and a throne was placed for the king’s mother. She sat at his right hand.
She said, “I have one small request to make of you. Do not refuse me.” The king said to her, “Ask, my mother, for I will not refuse you.”
She said to him, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife.”

King Solomon answered his mother, “Why do you ask for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for the kingdom for him as well, since he is my older brother, and Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah are on his side!”
King Solomon swore by the Lord, saying, “May God do this to me and more besides if Adonijah has not spoken these words at the cost of his own life!
Now, as the Lord lives, who has established me and seated me on the throne of my father David, and has made a house for me as he promised, Adonijah shall certainly be killed today.”
King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck Adonijah and killed him.

The king said to Abiathar the priest, “Go to Anathoth, to your own field, for you deserve death. But I will not put you to death today, because you carried the ark of the LORD before my father David and shared in his suffering everywhere he suffered.”
Solomon removed Abiathar from serving as priest to the LORD, fulfilling the word the LORD had spoken against the house of Eli at Shiloh.

The news that Adonijah had been killed reached Joab. Joab had sided with Adonijah and had not sided with Solomon. So Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and took refuge by grasping the horns of the altar.

King Solomon was told that Joab had fled to the tent of the LORD and had taken refuge by grasping the horns of the altar. King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada and told him, “Go, strike him down.”

Benaiah went into the tent of the LORD and said to him, “This is what the king says: ‘Come out.’” He said, “I will not come out. I will die here.” Benaiah reported this to the king, saying, “This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me.”
The king said, “Do to him as he has said. Strike him down and kill him, and remove from me and my father’s house the guilt for the innocent blood Joab shed.”

“May the LORD bring his blood back on his own head, because he attacked two men more righteous and better than himself and killed them with the sword without my father David knowing: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel’s army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah’s army.
May their blood come back on Joab’s head and on the heads of his descendants forever. But may David, his descendants, his house, and his throne have peace from the LORD forever.”
Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck him down, and killed him. He was buried in his tomb in the wilderness.
King Solomon appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in his place, and the king appointed Zadok the priest in Abiathar’s place.
The king sent for Shimei and said to him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there. Do not leave there to go anywhere else.
On the day you leave and cross the Kidron Valley, know for certain that you will die. Your blood will be on your own head.”
Shimei said to the king, “What you have said is good, my lord the king. Your servant will do so.” And Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.
After three years, two of Shimei’s servants fled to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. They told Shimei, “Look, your servants are in Gath.”
Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Achish at Gath to look for his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants back from Gath.
King Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned.

The king sent for Shimei and said to him, “Did I not make you swear by the LORD and warn you, saying, ‘On the day you leave Jerusalem and cross the Kidron Valley, know for certain that you will die’? And you said, ‘What you have said is good; I will do so.’”
Why did you not keep the oath sworn to the LORD and the command I gave you?
The king said to Shimei, “You know all the evil you did to my father David; your own heart knows it.
The LORD has brought your evil back on your own head. But King Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will be established before the LORD forever.”
The king gave orders to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck Shimei down, and he died. The kingdom was firmly established in Solomon’s hands.

Solomon became the son-in-law of Pharaoh king of Egypt. He married Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her into the City of David until he finished building his own house, the house of the LORD, and the wall all around Jerusalem.
However, the people were sacrificing at the high places, because no house for the name of the LORD had yet been built in those days.
Solomon loved the LORD and followed the commands of his father David, except that he sacrificed and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, because it was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar,
which was in Gibeon. Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in a vision at night, and God said to him, “Ask what I should give you.”

Solomon said, “You showed great kindness to your servant David my father, just as he walked before you in truth and faithfulness, and walked before you with an upright heart. You have kept this great kindness for him and have given him a son to sit on his throne, as is the case today.
And now, LORD God, you have made your servant king in place of my father David. But I am only a young boy and do not know how to go out or come in.
Among your people whom you have chosen, a great people who cannot be numbered or counted because they are so many.
Give your servant a listening heart to judge your people and to distinguish between good and evil. For who can judge this great people of yours?
This request pleased the Lord when Solomon asked for it.
The LORD said to Solomon, “Because you asked for this, and did not ask for wealth for yourself, or for the lives of your enemies, or for many days for yourself, but asked for wisdom to hear cases,”
Look, I have done as you asked. I have given you a wise and discerning heart, so that there has been no one like you before you, and no one like you will arise after you.
I have also given you what you did not ask for, both wealth and honor, so that no one among the kings will be like you throughout your life.
And if you walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and commandments, as your father David walked, I will prolong your life.

Solomon woke up and saw that it was a dream. He came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the Lord’s covenant. He offered burnt offerings and peace offerings and held a feast for all his servants.
Then two women who were prostitutes came before King Solomon for judgment.
One of the women said, “I beg you, my lord! This woman and I were living in the same house, and I gave birth while she was with me in the house.
Three days after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. We were together in the house, and no stranger was with us; only the two of us were in the house.
This woman’s son died during the night because she lay on him.
She got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me while your servant was asleep. She laid him in her arms and laid her dead son in my arms.
I got up in the morning to nurse my son and saw that he was dead. But when I looked closely at him in the morning, he was not the son I had given birth to.”

The other woman said, “No, that is not so! My son is the living one, and your son is the dead one.” The first woman said, “No, that is not so! Your son is the dead one, and my son is the living one.” They argued before the king.
The king said, “Bring me a sword.” So they brought a sword before the king.
The king said, “Cut the living child in two, and give half to one woman and half to the other.”

The woman whose son was alive spoke to the king, because she was overcome with compassion for her son. “I beg you, my lord! Give her the child alive, and do not kill him!” But the other woman said, “He shall be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!”
The king answered, “Give her the child alive, and do not kill him. She is his mother.”
All Israel heard about the judgment the king had given, and they stood in awe of the king, because they saw that God’s wisdom was in him to administer justice.
Solomon was king over all Israel.
These were his officials: Azariah son of Zadok, the priest;
Elihoreph and Ahijah, sons of Shisha, the scribes; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, the recorder;
Benaiah son of Jehoiada, in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar, priests;
Azariah son of Nathan, in charge of the governors; and Zabur son of Nathan, a priest and the king’s friend.
Abinshar was in charge of the royal household, and Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the tribute.
Solomon had these twelve governors over all Israel. They supplied food for the king, his household, and the army, each taking responsibility for providing supplies for one month of the year.
These were their names: Ben-hur in the hill country of Ephraim;
Ben-deker in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Aijalon of Beth-hanan;
Ben-hesed in Arubboth; Succoth and all the land of Hepher belonged to him;
Ben-abinadab in Naphath-dor. Taphath, Solomon’s daughter, was his wife;
Baana son of Ahilud in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean beside Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean as far as Abel-meholah and beyond Jokmeam;
Ben-geber in Ramoth-gilead; the region of Jair son of Manasseh belonged to him, as did the region of Argob in Bashan: sixty large towns with walls, gates, and bronze bars;
Ahinadab son of Gaddo in Mahanaim;
Ahimaaz in Naphtali; he too took a daughter of Solomon, Basemath, as his wife;
Baana son of Hushai in Asher and Bealoth;
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah in Issachar;
Shimei son of Ela in Benjamin;
Geber son of Uri in the land of Gilead, the land of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. Governors held authority in the land.
Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore, eating, drinking, and rejoicing.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the river of the land of the Philistines as far as the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.
Solomon’s provisions for a single day were thirty kors of fine flour and sixty kors of flour,
ten fattened oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened birds.
For he ruled over the whole region beyond the River, from Tiphsah as far as Gaza, and over all the kings beyond the River. He had peace on every side and all around him.
Judah and Israel lived in peace, each person under his vines and his fig trees, from Dan as far as Beersheba, throughout all Solomon’s days.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots and twelve thousand horsemen.
These governors supplied King Solomon and everyone who came to King Solomon’s table, each in his assigned month. They allowed nothing to be lacking.
They also brought barley and straw for the horses and mares to the place where he was, each according to his obligation.
God gave Solomon wisdom, understanding, and breadth of mind in very great abundance.
Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the East and all the wisdom of the Egyptians.
He was wiser than anyone—than Ethan the Easterner, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. His name became known among all the surrounding nations.
He spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs of praise numbered one thousand and five.
He spoke about trees, from the cedars of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He also spoke about animals, birds, creeping creatures, and fish.
People came from all nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom, from all the kings of the earth. He received gifts from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.

Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon, because he had heard that Solomon had been anointed king in place of his father, for Hiram had always loved David. Hiram sent a message to Solomon and blessed him.
Solomon sent word to Hiram, saying:
You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the many wars surrounding him, until the LORD put his enemies under the sole of his foot.
But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither an adversary nor any harmful occurrence.
Now I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to my father David: ‘Your son, whom I have placed on your throne in your place, will build a house for my name.’

Now give orders for cedar trees to be cut for me from Lebanon. My servants will work with your servants, and I will pay you whatever wages you specify for your servants. For you know that none of us knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.
When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he was very glad and said, ‘Blessed be the LORD today, who has given David a wise son to rule over this great people!’
Hiram sent word to Solomon, saying, “I have heard the message you sent me. I will fulfill all your wishes concerning cedar wood and cypress wood.”

My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will make them into rafts on the sea, taking them to the place you send word to me about. I will unload them there, and you will carry them away from there. You, in turn, will fulfill my wish by supplying food for my household.
Hiram supplied Solomon with cedar timber and cypress timber, as he desired.
Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household and twenty thousand kors of pressed oil. Solomon gave Hiram this amount every year.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon throughout their days, and the two of them made a covenant.
King Solomon raised a forced-labor levy from all Israel, and the levy numbered thirty thousand men.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand a month. They spent one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon had seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountains,
besides the officials whom Solomon appointed over the work: three thousand three hundred men who supervised the people doing the work.
The king gave orders, and they brought large stones, fine stones, to complete the house with dressed stone.
Solomon’s builders, Hiram’s builders, and the master craftsmen cut and prepared the stones and timber for building the house.

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Iyar, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD.
The house that Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
The porch in front of the entrance to the house was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the width of the house, and ten cubits wide, extending in the direction of the house’s length.
He made splayed, enclosed windows for the house.
He built rooms against the walls of the house, all around its walls, surrounding the main hall and the chamber of atonement. He made rooms all around.

The lowest room was five cubits wide, the middle one six cubits wide, and the third seven cubits wide, because ledges had been made around the outside of the house so that the walls would be joined to one another.
When the house was being built, it was built with stones fully prepared at the quarry. Neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.
The entrance to the middle chamber was on the south side of the temple. A winding staircase led up to the middle story, and from the middle story they went up to the third.
He built the temple and finished it, roofing it with beams and sawn cedar planks.
He built chambers around the whole temple, five cubits high, and attached them to the temple with cedar timbers.
The word of the Lord came to Solomon, saying:

“As for this temple that you have built, if you walk in my statutes, keep my judgments, carry out all my commandments, and follow them, I will fulfill with you the promises that I made to David your father.
I will dwell among the Israelites and will not abandon my people Israel.”
Solomon built the temple and completed it.
He lined the temple’s interior walls with cedar boards. From its floor to its ceiling he covered the inside with wood, and he covered the temple’s floor with cypress boards.
Solomon enclosed twenty cubits at the rear of the temple with cedar boards, from its floor to its ceiling, and built this inner section as the Holy of Holies.
The house, the inner temple, was forty cubits long.
The temple was lined inside with cedar, carved with rings, [?], and lilies. It was all cedar, and no stone could be seen in it.
He prepared the sanctuary inside the temple to place there the ark of the covenant of the Lord.
He lined the sanctuary, which was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. He overlaid it with refined gold, and he covered the altar with cedar.
Solomon overlaid the inside of the temple with refined gold. He made a partition in front of the sanctuary and overlaid it with gold.
He overlaid the entire temple with gold until the whole temple was finished. He also overlaid the entire altar belonging to the sanctuary with gold.
In the sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, measuring ten cubits in length.
The width of one cherub was five cubits, and the wing of the other cherub was five cubits. From one wingtip to the other was ten cubits.
The other cherub also measured ten cubits. Both cherubim had the same measurements and the same stature.
The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and the other cherub was the same.

He placed the cherubim inside the inner chamber and spread out their wings. The wing of one touched one wall, and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall. Their wings in the middle of the temple touched one another.
He overlaid the cherubim with refined gold.
He surrounded all the temple’s walls with rings and carved [?], cherubim, palm trees, and lilies, both inside and outside.
He overlaid the temple’s floor with gold, both inside and outside.
For the entrance to the sanctuary he made doors of olivewood, with their doorframes firmly secured and strengthened.
The two doors were of olivewood, and carved on them were cherubim, [?], palm trees, and lilies. He overlaid them with gold and applied extra gold to the cherubim and palm trees.
Likewise, for the entrance to the main hall he made its doorframes of olivewood, plain and square.
And two doors of cypress wood: the two panels of one door were carved, and the two panels of the other door were carved.
He carved cherubim, [?], palm trees, and lilies, and overlaid the fine carving with gold.
He built the inner courtyard with three courses of dressed stone and one course of cedar beams.
In the fourth year, in the month of Iyar, the foundation of the house of the Lord was laid.
In the eleventh year, in the month of Second Tishri, which is the eighth month, the house was completed in all its details and all its workmanship. He built it in seven years.
Solomon built his own house over thirteen years, and the entire house was completed.
He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high, on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.
It was roofed with cedar above the beams resting on the pillars—forty-five in all, fifteen to a row.
There were three rows of galleries, facing one another in three tiers.
All the doorways and thresholds were rectangular, facing one another in three tiers.
He made the portico of pillars fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide, with a portico in front of the pillars and a courtyard in front of them.
He made the portico of the throne, where he would judge, as a portico for judgment, and covered it with cedar from its foundations to its ceiling.

His own house, where he lived, was in another courtyard, farther inside than the porch, and he built it in the same style. He also built a house in the same style for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom Solomon had married.
All these were fine stones, dressed to measure and cut with a saw on the inside and outside, from the foundations to the top, and outside as far as the courtyard of the house.
It was constructed of fine stones and large stones, stones measuring ten cubits and stones measuring eight cubits.
Above were fine stones, dressed to measure, and cedar.
The great courtyard had three courses of dressed stone and one course of cedar beams all around, as did the inner courtyard of the house of the Lord and the portico of the house.
King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.

He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a Tyrian man, a craftsman in bronze. He was filled with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge for doing every kind of bronze work. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.
He fashioned two bronze pillars. One pillar was eighteen cubits high, and a cord twelve cubits long encircled it. The other pillar was the same.
He made two capitals of cast bronze to place on top of the pillars. One capital was five cubits high, and the other capital was five cubits high.
He made latticework, woven latticework, and made chains for the capitals on top of the pillars: seven for one capital and seven for the other capital.
He made the pillars and two rows all around one lattice to cover the capitals on top of the pillars, and likewise for the other pillar.
The capitals on top of the pillars were fashioned like lilies, and he made them four cubits high in the portico.
The capitals on the two pillars were also above, opposite the side facing the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows around one capital, and likewise around the other capital.
He made the pillars of the temple portico. He set up the pillar on the right and named it Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the left and named it Boaz.
On top of the pillars was lily-shaped work. Thus the work on the pillars was completed.
He made the sea of cast metal, ten cubits from rim to rim, round all around, and five cubits high. A cord thirty cubits long encircled it.
Gourds below its rim encircled it all around, extending ten cubits around the sea. There were two rows of gourds, cast in the same casting.
It stood on twelve oxen: three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea rested above them, on top of them, and their hindquarters faced inward.
Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its rim was like the rim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It held two thousand measures.
He made ten bronze stands. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
This was the construction of the stands: they had panels.
On the panels between the crossbars were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the coverings above there were similar designs, and below the lions and oxen was a design of fine workmanship.
Each stand had four bronze wheels and a bronze axle. Their four corners were joined together, and they had supports underneath them—cast supports of fine workmanship.
The opening of the stand measured a cubit on the inside. Its opening was round, measuring a cubit and a half. There were also carvings on its opening, and its panels were square, not round.
The four wheels were below the panels, and the wheel axles were attached to each stand. Each wheel was a cubit and a half high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels. Their axles, sides, ornaments, and embellishments were cast.
There were four supports at the four corners of each stand; its supports were formed from the stands themselves.
The body of the stand was half a cubit high and round all around. At the top of the stand, its handles and panels were of one piece with it.
He engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees all around on the plates of its handles and on its panels.
This was how he made the ten stands. They all had the same casting, the same measurements, and the same shape.
He made ten bronze basins. Each basin held forty measures and measured four cubits. There was one basin on each stand, and so it was for all ten stands.
He placed five of the stands on the right side of the house and five on the left side of the house. He placed the sea on the southeast side of the house, facing south.
Hiram made the basins, pots, shovels, and bowls. Hiram finished doing all the work that he did for King Solomon in the house of the Lord.
The two pillars, the two bowls on top of the pillars, and the two coverings to cover the two bowls on top of the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two coverings, with two rows of pomegranates for each covering, to cover the two openings of the bowls on top of the pillars;
the ten stands and the ten basins on the stands;
the one sea and the twelve oxen beneath the sea;
the pots, shovels, bowls, and all the utensils for service that Hiram made for King Solomon for the house of the Lord were of Corinthian bronze.
In the plain in the valley of Jericho, beside the Jordan, the king cast them in the finest earth, between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon made all these utensils in such great abundance that there was no reckoning of the weight of the bronze.
King Solomon made for the house of the Lord all the furnishings of the house of the Lord: the gold altar and the gold table on which was the bread of the Presence.
And the lampstands of pure gold, five on the right and five on the left before the temple, and the spoons, lamps, and tongs of gold.
And the bowls, snuffers, basins, spoons, and censers of pure gold, and the gold covering of the inner door of the Holy of Holies and of the door of the temple building.

All the work that King Solomon did on the house of the Lord was completed. Solomon brought the things his father David had dedicated—the silver, gold, and utensils—and placed them in the treasury of the house of the Lord.

Then Solomon assembled all the tribes of Israel, all the heads of the tribes, and the leaders of the ancestral families. They gathered before King Solomon in Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the city of David, which is Zion.
All the people of Israel gathered before King Solomon in the month of the harvest, at the festival, which is in the seventh month.
All the tribes of Israel came, and the priests lifted up the ark of the Lord.
They brought it up to the temple of the Lord, together with the tent of meeting and the sacred utensils of the tent. The priests of Israel and the Levites went up with them.
King Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel who had gathered before him stood with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle too numerous to be counted or reckoned.
The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord to its place in the temple, into the chamber of the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
For the cherubim spread their wings in the holy place, sheltering the ark and its poles from above with their wings.
The poles were long, and their ends could be seen from the holy place in front of the temple, but they could not be seen from outside. They have remained there to this day.
There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses placed there at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the Israelites as they came out of Egypt.
When the priests came out of the holy place, a cloud filled the house of the Lord.
The priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.
Then Solomon said, “Lord, you said that you would dwell in thick darkness.
I have indeed built a house, a dwelling for you, a place prepared for you to live in forever.”
The king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, while the whole assembly of Israel stood.
He said, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to my father David and fulfilled it with his hands, saying,

‘From the day I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I did not choose a city from any of the tribes of Israel in which to build a house where my name would be. But I chose David to rule over my people Israel.’
My father David had it in his heart to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.
But the Lord said to my father David, ‘Because you had it in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well to have this in your heart.
Nevertheless, you will not build a house for my name. Rather, your son, who will come from your own body, will build a house for my name.’

The Lord has fulfilled the word he spoke. I have succeeded my father David and have sat on the throne of Israel, as the Lord said, and I have built a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.
There I have placed the ark of the covenant of the Lord, which he made with our ancestors when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.”
Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord, facing the whole assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven.

He prayed and said, “Lord, God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below. You keep your covenant and show kindness to your servants who walk faithfully before you with all their heart and all their soul.
You have kept what you promised your servant David my father. You spoke with your mouth and fulfilled it with your hands, as it is today.

And now, LORD, God of Israel, keep what you promised your servant David my father, saying, “You will never lack a son before me to sit on the throne of Israel, provided that your sons watch their ways and walk faithfully before me, as you have walked before me.”
And now, LORD, God of Israel, let the word you swore to your servant David my father be confirmed.
But will God really dwell on earth? Look, heaven and the highest heavens cannot contain you, much less this house that I have built!
Turn toward your servant’s prayer and his plea, LORD my God, and listen to the plea and prayer that your servant offers before you today.
May your eyes be open toward this house day and night, toward the place where you said, “My name will be there,” to hear the prayer that your servant prays before you toward this place.
Hear the plea of your servant and of your people Israel when they pray before you in this place. You, our God, hear from your dwelling place, from heaven, and forgive.
If someone sins against his neighbor and is required to take an oath, and comes and swears before your altar in this house,
then hear from heaven, act, and judge your servants, condemning the guilty and bringing his conduct down on his own head, and vindicating the innocent and rewarding him according to his innocence.
When your people Israel are defeated in battle by enemies because they have sinned against you, and they turn back to you, acknowledge your name, pray, and plead with you in this place,
then hear from heaven, forgive the sins of your servants and your people Israel, and bring them back to the land you gave their ancestors.
When the heavens are shut and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, and they come and pray in this place, acknowledge your name, and turn from their sins when you afflict them,

then hear from heaven and forgive the sins of your servants and your people Israel, teaching them the good way in which they should walk. Give your rain on the land you gave your people as an inheritance.
When there is famine in the land, or plague, blight, mildew, locusts, or devouring locusts, or when enemies besiege them in any of their cities, whatever the disease or affliction,
whatever prayer or plea is made by anyone among all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and spreading out his hands before you in this house,
then hear from heaven, your established dwelling place, forgive, act, and give to each person according to his ways, for you know his heart. You alone know the hearts of all human beings.
So that they may fear you all the days they live on the land you gave to their ancestors.
Also concerning the foreigner who is not of your people Israel and comes from a distant land because of your name—
when they hear of your great name, your mighty hand, and your uplifted arm, and he comes and prays before you in this house,

then hear from heaven, your established dwelling place, and do what the foreigner calls on you to do, so that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you as your people Israel do, and may know that this house I have built bears your name.
When your people go out to battle against their enemies, wherever you send them, and pray before you, LORD, toward the city you have favored and this house I have built for your name,
Hear their prayer and their plea from heaven, and uphold their cause.

when they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and you become angry with them and hand them over to their enemies, and their captors carry them away to their enemies’ land, far away or nearby,
and they take it to heart in the land where they have been taken captive, repent, and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, “We have sinned, done wrong, and acted wickedly,”

and they turn back to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies who took them captive, and pray before you toward their land, which you gave their ancestors, the city you chose, and the house I have built for your name,
then hear their prayer and their plea from heaven, your established dwelling place, and uphold their cause.
Forgive your people for sinning against you and for all the offenses they have committed against you. Grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors, so that they may have mercy on them.
For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of Egypt, out of the iron furnace.
May your eyes be open to the plea of your servants and your people Israel, and may you hear them whenever they call to you.
For you set them apart for yourself as an inheritance from all the peoples of the earth, as you declared through your servant Moses when you brought their ancestors out of Egypt, O Lord God.
When Solomon had finished offering all this prayer and supplication before the Lord God, he rose from before the Lord’s altar, where he had been kneeling with his hands spread out toward heaven.
He stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, saying in a loud voice:
“Blessed is the Lord God, who has given rest to his people Israel, as he promised. Not one word has failed of all the good promises he made through his servant Moses.
May the Lord our God be with us as he was with our ancestors. May he not abandon us or leave us,
but turn our hearts toward him, to walk in his ways and keep his commandments, statutes, and judgments, which he commanded our ancestors.
May these words with which I have pleaded before the Lord remain near the Lord God night and day, so that he may uphold the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, day by day,
so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God and that there is no other besides him.
May your hearts be wholly devoted to the Lord our God, to walk in his ways and keep his commandments, statutes, judgments, and laws, as you do today.”
King Solomon and all Israel with him were offering a great sacrifice before the Lord.
Solomon offered sacrifices of peace offerings before the Lord: twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the Israelites dedicated the Lord’s house.

On that day the king consecrated the inner part of the courtyard in front of the Lord’s house, because he offered the burnt offerings, the offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings there. For the bronze altar before the Lord was too small to hold the burnt offerings, the offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings.

At that time Solomon celebrated the festival, and all Israel with him, gathered from the entrance of Hamath to the entrance of the brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, for seven days and another seven days—fourteen days.

On the eighth day he sent the people away. They blessed the king and went to their tents, joyful and glad at heart because of all the good things the Lord had done for his servant David and his people Israel.
When Solomon had finished building the Lord’s house and the king’s house, and everything else Solomon wished to do,
the Lord appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.

The Lord said to him, “I have heard your prayer and the plea you have made before me. I have consecrated for myself this house you have built, to put my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there always.
As for you, if you walk before me as your father David walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing as I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and judgments,
I will establish the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, as I promised your father David: ‘You will never lack a man on the throne of Israel.’
But if you and your children turn away from following me and do not keep my commandments and statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,

I will destroy Israel from the face of the land I have given them, and I will uproot from my presence the house I have consecrated for my name. Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all the peoples.
This house will become a ruin. Everyone who passes by it will be appalled and hiss, and they will say, ‘Why has the Lord done this to this land and this house?’

They will say, “Because they abandoned the LORD their God, who brought their ancestors out of the land of Egypt, and embraced the gods of other nations, served them, and worshiped them. That is why the LORD brought all this disaster upon them.”
After twenty years, during which Solomon built the two houses—the Lord’s house and the king’s house—
Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar timber, cypress timber, and gold, as much as he wanted. Then King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee.
Hiram came out from Tyre to see the towns Solomon had given him, but they did not please him.
He said, “What are these towns you have given me, my brother?” He called them the land of Cabul, as they are called to this day.
King Hiram sent King Solomon 120 talents of gold.
This is the account of the tribute King Solomon raised to build the house of the Lord and his own house. He also built the wall of Jerusalem, Millo, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up, captured Gezer, burned it with fire, and killed the Canaanites living in the town. He gave it as a gift to his daughter, Solomon’s wife.
Solomon rebuilt Gezer and Lower Beth-horon,
and Baalath and Tadmor in the wilderness country,
and all Solomon’s storage towns, the towns for his chariots, and the towns for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon wished to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the land under his rule.
All the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not Israelites—
their descendants who remained after them, whom the Israelites had been unable to destroy—Solomon made into tribute-paying slaves, as they remain to this day.
But Solomon did not make slaves of the Israelites, because they were his warriors, his servants, his officials, his mighty men, and the commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
These were the overseers in charge of Solomon’s work: 550 men who supervised the people and made them carry out the work.
Pharaoh’s daughter went up from the city of David to the house Solomon had built for her. Then he built Millo.
Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar before the Lord, and he placed incense on it before the Lord. So he completed the house.
King Solomon built a ship at Ezion-geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Arvad.
King Hiram sent his servants aboard the ship, sailors who knew the sea, along with Solomon’s servants.
They went to Ophir, took 420 talents of gold from there, and brought it to King Solomon.
The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame and the name of the Lord, and she came to test him with riddles.

She came to Jerusalem with a very large retinue, with camels carrying spices, a very great quantity of gold, and precious stones. She came to King Solomon and tested him with everything she had in mind.
Solomon explained everything to her. Nothing was hidden from the king that he could not explain to her.
The queen of Sheba saw all Solomon’s wisdom and the house he had built,

the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance of his ministers and their clothing, his cupbearers and their clothing, and the burnt offerings he offered in the house of the Lord. She was left breathless.
She said to the king, “The report I heard in my own land about your words and your wisdom was true.
But I did not believe the reports until I came and saw with my own eyes. And look, I was not told even half! Your wisdom and prosperity exceed the report I heard.
How fortunate your wives are! How fortunate these servants of yours are, who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom!
Blessed be the LORD your God, who took pleasure in you and seated you on the throne of Israel. Because the LORD loves Israel forever, he made you king to administer justice and righteousness.
She gave King Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of gold, a very large quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again did spices arrive like those that the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.
Hiram's ships also carried gold from Ophir and brought from Ophir a very large quantity of boxwood and precious stones.
King Solomon used the boxwood to make ornaments for the house of the LORD and the king's palace, and lyres and harps for the singers. No boxwood like that has been brought or seen to this day.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and requested, besides what he gave her with royal generosity. Then she returned to her own land, she and her servants.
The weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold,
apart from what came from craftsmen, the commerce of merchants, all the kings of the Arabs, and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of refined gold. He applied six hundred minas of gold to each large shield.
He also made three hundred shields of refined gold. He applied three hundred minas of gold to each shield, and the king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with gold from Ophir.
He made six steps for the throne. The top of the throne was rounded at the back, and there were armrests on either side of the seat, with two lions standing on either side.
Twelve lions stood beside the six steps, on either side. Nothing like it had been made in any kingdom.
All the vessels used in King Solomon's service were gold, and all the vessels in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were refined gold. Silver was considered worth nothing in Solomon's days.
For the king had ships of Tarshish at sea with Hiram's ships. Once every three years a ship came from Tarshish carrying silver, gold, elephants, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom.
All the kings of the earth sought to see Solomon and hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart.
Each brought his gift: vessels of gold, vessels of silver, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, carriages, and mules, year after year.
King Solomon assembled chariots and horsemen. He had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed the chariots in towns, with some of them alongside the king in Jerusalem.
King Solomon made silver as plentiful as stones in Jerusalem, and cedars as plentiful as the sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Solomon's horses came from Egypt. The king's merchants received a fee; they bought them at a price.

A chariot was brought up from Egypt for six hundred pieces of silver, and a horse for one hundred and fifty. Likewise, all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Edom brought in large numbers through their agents.
King Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh's daughter, and Ammonite, Moabite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women.

They were from the nations about which the LORD had told the Israelites, 'You must not mingle with them, nor may they mingle with you, lest they turn your hearts after their gods.' Solomon clung to these women, held fast to them, and loved them.
He had seven hundred wives of noble birth and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned his heart astray.
When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods. His heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of his father David had been.
Solomon followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, the idol of the Moabites, and Milcom, the god of the Ammonites.
Solomon did what was evil before the LORD and did not follow the LORD wholeheartedly as his father David had.
Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain opposite Jerusalem, and for Milcom, the idol of the Ammonites.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and offered sacrifices to their gods.
The Lord was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the Lord, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
He had commanded him about this matter, telling him not to follow the gods of the nations, but Solomon did not keep what the Lord had commanded him.

The Lord said to Solomon, “Because you have done this and have not kept my statutes, my judgments, and my commandments that I commanded you, I will certainly tear the kingdom from your hand and give it to your servant.
However, I will not do it during your lifetime, for the sake of David my servant. I will tear it from your son’s hand.
But I will not tear away the whole kingdom. I will give your son one tribe, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen.”
The Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, who was of the royal line in Edom.
When David devastated Edom, when Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain and killed every male in Edom,
For Joab stayed there for six months, with all Israel alongside him, until he had killed every male in Edom.
Hadad fled with some Edomite men from among his father’s servants to go to Egypt. Hadad was a small boy.

They set out from Midian and went to Paran. They took men with them from Paran and went to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt. He gave Hadad a house and food and said to him, “Stay with me.” He also gave him land.
Hadad found favor in Pharaoh’s eyes, and Pharaoh gave him his wife’s sister, the sister of Queen Tahpenes, as his wife.
The sister of Tahpenes bore him his son Genubath. Tahpenes weaned him in Pharaoh’s house, and Genubath lived in Pharaoh’s house among Pharaoh’s sons.
While in Egypt, Hadad heard that David had rested with his ancestors and that Joab the commander of the army had died. Hadad said to Pharaoh, “Let me leave and go to my own land.”
Pharaoh said to him, “What have you lacked here with me that you now want to go away to your own land?” He answered him, “Nothing, but please do let me leave.”
The Lord raised up another adversary against him: Hadron son of Eliada, who had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah.
Men gathered around him, and he became the leader of a raiding band. When David killed them, they went to Damascus and settled there, and Hadad became king in Damascus.
He was an adversary of Israel throughout Solomon’s lifetime because of the evil he did. Hadad oppressed the Israelites and ruled over Edom.
Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephrathite from Zedad, whose mother was a widow named Zeruah, was a servant of Solomon. He rebelled against King Solomon.
This was the reason he rebelled against King Solomon: Solomon was building the Millo and closing the breaches in the city of David.
Jeroboam was a capable man. King Solomon saw that the young man was capable and put him in charge of all the labor of the house of Joseph.
At that time, Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the open country.
Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces.
He said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces for yourself, for this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘Look, I am tearing the kingdom from Solomon’s hand, and I will give you ten tribes.
But he will have one tribe, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I chose out of all the tribes of Israel.

This is because he has abandoned me and worshiped Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, the god of the Moabites, and Milcom, the god of the Ammonites. He has not walked in my ways or done what is right in my sight, nor has he kept my statutes and my judgments as his father David did.

But I will not take the whole kingdom from his hands. Instead, I will keep him as ruler throughout his lifetime, for the sake of David my servant, whom I chose and who kept my commandments and my statutes.
I will take the kingdom from his son's hands and give you ten tribes.
But I will give his son one tribe, so that my servant David may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city I chose for myself to put my name there.
I will give it to you, and you will reign as you desire and be king over Israel.

If you obey everything I have commanded you, walk in my ways, do what is right before me, and keep my statutes and commandments as my servant David did, I will be with you. I will build you an enduring house, as I built for my servant David, and I will give Israel to you.
I will humble David's descendants because of this, but not forever.
Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and remained in Egypt until Solomon died.
The rest of Solomon's deeds, everything he did, and his wisdom are recorded in the book of Solomon's deeds.
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.
Solomon rested with his ancestors and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam became king after him.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.
When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard—he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon, and Jeroboam was living in Egypt—
they sent for him and summoned him. Jeroboam and all the people of Israel came and said to Rehoboam,
"Your father made our yoke harsh. Now lighten the harsh service your father demanded and the heavy yoke he laid on us, and we will serve you."
Rehoboam said to them, "Go away, and come back to me three days from now." So all the people went away.
King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father while he was alive. He said to them, "How do you advise me to answer these people?"
They said to him, "If today you become a servant to these people and serve them, answer them, and speak kindly to them, they will be your servants forever."
He rejected the advice the elders had given him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him.
He said to them, "What answer do you advise me to give these people who say to me, 'Lighten the yoke your father laid on us'?"

The young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Say this to the people who told you, 'Your father made our yoke harsh; lighten it for us.' Tell them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's waist.
My father imposed a heavy yoke on you; I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with rods.'"
Jeroboam and all Israel came to Rehoboam on the third day, just as the king had told them, "Come back to me on the third day."
The king answered the people harshly and rejected the advice the elders had given him.
He spoke to them according to the young men's advice: "My father made your yoke heavy; I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with rods."

The king did not listen to the people, for the provocation came from the LORD, so that the LORD might fulfill the words he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the prophet from Shiloh concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat.

All Israel saw that the king would not listen to them. The people answered the king, saying, "We have no share in David and no inheritance with the son of Jesse. To your tents, Israel! Now look after your own house, David!" So the Israelites went away, each to his own town.
The Israelites were living in their towns, and Judah made Rehoboam son of Solomon king over them.
King Rehoboam sent Adoniram, who was in charge of the tribute, to all Israel. But all the people of Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam managed to get into a chariot and flee to Jerusalem.
So the house of Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him, summoned him to the assembly, and made him king over all Israel. No one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone.

Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, and all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin assembled—180,000 fighting men—to fight against the house of Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.
The word of the LORD came to Shemaiah, the prophet of God, saying:
“Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and the rest of the people:

‘This is what the LORD says: Do not go up or fight against your brothers, the people of Israel. Return, each of you, to your home, for this has come about through me.’” They listened to the word of the LORD and turned back to leave, according to the word of the LORD.
Jeroboam built up Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. He went out from there and built up Penuel.
Jeroboam said to himself, “Now the kingdom will return to the house of David.

If these people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah. They will kill me and return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah.”

The king took counsel and made two golden calves. He said to all Israel, “It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem.” And he said, “Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.”
He placed one in Bethel and the other in Dan.
This became a sin, and the people went all the way to Dan to worship before one of them.
He built a house of high places and appointed priests from among the people who were not descendants of Levi.

Jeroboam established a festival in the eighth month, at the full moon of that month, like the festival in Judah, and he went up to the altar. He did the same in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves he had made. In Bethel he appointed priests for the high places he had made.

He went up to the altar he had made in Bethel, at the full moon in the eighth month, in the month he had devised in his own heart. He established a festival for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to offer incense.
And look, a prophet of God came from Judah to Bethel by the word of the LORD, while Jeroboam was standing at the altar to offer incense.

He proclaimed the word of the LORD against the altar and said, “Altar, altar, hear the word of the LORD! This is what the LORD says: A son will be born to the house of David, named Josiah. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who offer incense on you, and on you he will burn human bones.”
That day he gave a sign, saying, “This is the sign that the LORD has sent me: The altar will split apart, and the ashes on it will be poured out.”

When the king heard the words that the prophet of God proclaimed against the altar in Bethel, the king stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!” But the hand he stretched out against him withered, and he could not draw it back.
The altar split apart, and the ashes on it were poured out, according to the sign that the prophet of God had given by the word of the LORD.

The king said to the prophet of God, “Pray for me before the LORD your God, and plead for me so that my hand may be restored to me.” The prophet of God prayed before the LORD, and the king’s hand was restored to him and became as it had been before.
The king said to the prophet of God, “Come home with me and eat, and I will give you gifts.”
The prophet of God said to him, “Even if you give me half your estate, I will not go into your house with you, nor will I eat bread or drink water.
For this is what the LORD commanded me by his word. He said to me, ‘Do not eat bread or drink water, and do not return by the road you came on.’”
So he went away by another road and did not return by the road on which he had come to Bethel.
An old prophet lived in Bethel. His sons came and told him everything that the prophet of God had done that day in Bethel. His sons also told their father the words he had spoken to the king.
Their father asked them, “Which way did he go?” His sons showed him the road taken by the prophet of God who had come from Judah.
He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” They saddled the donkey for him, and he mounted it.
He went after the prophet of God and found him sitting under a terebinth tree. He asked him, “Are you the prophet of God who came from Judah?” He replied, “I am.”
He said to him, “Come home with me and eat bread.”
He replied, “I cannot return with you or come to your house. I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.
For this is what I was told by the word of the Lord: ‘Do not eat bread there or drink water there, and do not return by the road you came on.’”
He said to him, “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel told me by the word of the Lord, ‘Bring him back with you to your house so that he may eat bread and drink water.’” But he was lying to him.
So he returned with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water.
While they were sitting at the table, the word of the Lord came to the prophet who had brought him back.

He called out to the prophet of God who had come from Judah and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Because you rebelled against the word spoken by the Lord and did not keep the command that the Lord your God gave you,
but returned and ate bread and drank water in the place where I told you not to eat bread or drink water, your body will not enter the tomb of your ancestors.’”
After they had eaten bread and drunk water, they saddled the donkey for the prophet of God.
He set off on his return journey, and a lion met him on the road and killed him. His body lay on the road, with the donkey standing beside it and the lion standing beside the body.
Some people passing by saw the body lying on the road, with the donkey standing beside it and the lion standing beside the body. They came and reported it in the town where the old prophet lived.

When the prophet who had brought him back from his journey heard this, he said, “It is the prophet of God. Because he disobeyed the word spoken by the Lord, the Lord handed him over to the lion, which mauled him and killed him, in accordance with the word the Lord spoke to him.”
He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me,” and they saddled it for him.
He went and found the body lying on the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey.
The prophet picked up the body of the prophet of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it to the town where he himself, the old prophet, lived, to mourn over him and bury him.
He laid his body in the tomb and mourned over him, saying, “Alas, my brother! Alas, my brother!”
After they had buried him, he said to his sons, “When I die, bury me in the tomb where the prophet of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones.
For the message he proclaimed by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines of the high places in the city of Samaria will certainly come true.”

After this event, Jeroboam did not turn from his evil ways. Once again he appointed priests for the high places from among the people. Whoever wanted to become a priest presented an offering and became a priest of a high place.
This became a sin for the house of Jeroboam, leading to its uprooting and destruction from the face of the earth.
At that time Abijah, the son of Jeroboam, became ill.

Jeroboam said to his wife, “Get up and disguise yourself so that no one will know you are Jeroboam’s wife. Go to Shiloh. The prophet Ahijah is there; he is the one who told me that I would reign over this people.
Take with you ten loaves of bread, cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what will happen to the boy.”
Jeroboam’s wife did so. She got up, went to Shiloh, and entered Ahijah’s house. Ahijah could not see anything, because his eyes had grown dim with old age.
The LORD said to Ahijah, “Jeroboam’s wife is coming to ask you about her son, who is sick. Say such and such to her. When she comes in, she will be disguised.”
When Ahijah heard the sound of her footsteps as she entered the doorway, he said to her, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam! Why are you disguised? I have been sent to you with harsh news.
Go and tell Jeroboam, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I raised you up from among the people and made you ruler over my people Israel.’

I tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you. But you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing what was right in my sight.
But you have done more evil than all who were before you. You went and made cast-metal gods for yourself to provoke me to anger, and you cast me behind your back.

Therefore, I am bringing disaster on the house of Jeroboam. I will destroy every male of Jeroboam’s household who urinates against a wall, whether confined or free in Israel. I will clear away the house of Jeroboam as the vines of a vineyard are cleared away when the grape harvest is finished.
The dogs will eat anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city, and the birds of the sky will eat anyone belonging to him who dies in the open country, for the LORD has spoken.
As for you, get up and go home. When your feet enter the city, the boy will die.

All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. He alone of Jeroboam’s household will be laid in a grave, because in him, among the household of Jeroboam, something good was found before the LORD, the God of Israel.
The LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who will destroy the house of Jeroboam from this day on—and what now?

The LORD will strike Israel like a reed shaken by the wind. He will uproot Israel from this good land that he gave their ancestors and scatter them beyond the River, because they made idols for themselves and provoked the LORD to anger.
He will give Israel up because of the sins that Jeroboam committed and caused Israel to commit.”
Jeroboam’s wife got up, went away, and entered Tirzah. As she entered the doorway of her house, the boy died.
All Israel mourned for him and buried him, according to the word of the LORD, which he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the prophet, the Shilonite.
The rest of Jeroboam’s deeds, how he fought and how he reigned, are recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Jeroboam reigned over Israel for twenty-two years. Then Jeroboam rested with his ancestors, and his son Nadab succeeded him as king.

Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned over Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite.
Judah did what was evil in the LORD’s sight. They provoked him to jealousy with everything their ancestors had done and with the sins they committed.
They too built high places, sacred pillars, and idols for themselves on every high hill and under every leafy tree.
There was also prostitution in the land, and they practiced all the abominations of the nations that the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt marched against Jerusalem.
He took the treasures of the LORD’s house and the treasures of the royal palace. He also took all the gold shields Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and entrusted them to the commanders and the runners who guarded the entrance to the royal palace.
Whenever the king entered the LORD’s house, the runners carried the shields and brought them to the guardhouse.
The rest of Rehoboam’s deeds and everything he did are recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.
Rehoboam rested with his ancestors and was buried in the city of David. His son Abijah became king in his place.
In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijah became king over Judah.
He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah daughter of Absalom.
He followed all the sins his father had committed before him, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the Lord his God, as the heart of his father David had been.
For the sake of his ancestor David, the Lord God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem by raising up his son after him and establishing him in Jerusalem.
For David had done what was right before the Lord his God and had not turned aside from anything he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
There was war between Abijah son of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of their lives.
The rest of Abijah’s deeds and everything he did are recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
Abijah rested with his ancestors and was buried in the city of David. His son Asa became king in his place.
In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa became king of Judah.
He reigned in Jerusalem for forty-one years. His mother's name was Maacah daughter of Absalom.
Asa did what was right before the Lord, as his father David had done.
He removed the prostitutes from the land and removed all the idols his ancestors had made.
He also removed his mother Maacah from her high position because she had held a festival for her deity. Asa cut down her idol and burned it in the Kidron Valley.
He did not remove the high places, but Asa's heart was fully devoted to the Lord his God all his days.
He brought the sacred gifts of his ancestors and his own sacred gifts into the house of the Lord: silver, gold, and utensils.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.
Then Baasha king of Israel marched against Judah and fortified Ramah, allowing no one to go out from or come in to Asa king of Judah.

Asa took all the silver and gold that remained in the house of the Lord and in the treasury of the royal palace and entrusted it to his servants. Asa king of Judah sent them to Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, king of Edom, who lived in Damascus, saying:

“There is a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Look, I have sent you a gift of silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel so that he will withdraw from me.”
Ben-hadad listened to Asa and sent his army commanders against the cities of Israel. They destroyed Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all the cities throughout the land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and stayed in Tirzah.
King Asa summoned all Judah, with no one exempted. They carried away the stones and timber of Ramah with which Baasha had been building. With these King Asa fortified Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.

The rest of Asa's deeds, all his mighty acts, everything he did, and the cities he built are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. In his old age, Asa developed a disease in his feet.
Asa rested with his ancestors and was buried with his ancestors in the city of his ancestor David. His son Jehoshaphat became king in his place.
Nadab son of Jeroboam became king over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah. He reigned over Israel for two years.
He did what was evil before the Lord and followed his father's ways and the sins by which his father had led Israel into sin.
Baasha son of Ahijah, from the house of Issachar, rebelled against him and killed him at Gath, which belonged to the Philistines. Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gath.
Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and became king in his place.

When he became king, he struck down the entire house of Jeroboam. He left no one alive in Jeroboam’s house, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the prophet, the Shilonite.
This was because of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins he committed and caused Israel to commit, greatly provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger.
