The rest of Nadab’s deeds and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
There was war between Baasha and Asa king of Judah throughout their lives.
In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned for twenty-four years.
He did what was evil before the Lord and followed the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins he had caused Israel to commit.
The word of the Lord came to Jehu son of Hanani concerning Baasha, saying:

“This is what the Lord says: Because I raised you from the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel, but you followed the ways of Jeroboam and caused my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger by the work of their hands,
look, I will sweep away Baasha’s descendants and his household, and I will make his house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
The dogs will eat anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city, and the birds of the sky will eat anyone belonging to him who dies in the open country.”
The rest of Baasha’s deeds, everything he did, and all his might are recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Baasha lay down with his ancestors and was buried in Tirzah. His son Elah became king after him.

The word of the Lord also came through Jehu son of Hanani the prophet against Baasha and his entire house, because of all the evil he had done before the Lord, provoking him to anger by the work of his hands and becoming like the house of Jeroboam, and because he had killed him.
In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned for two years.
His servant Zimri, commander of half the chariots, rebelled against him. He was in Tirzah, drinking aged wine in the house of [?], which he had built in Tirzah.
Zimri entered, struck him down, and killed him in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah. He became king after him.
When he became king and sat on his throne, he struck down the entire house of Baasha. He left him no one who urinates against a wall, nor any of his relatives or friends.
Zimri destroyed the entire house of Baasha according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet.
This was because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of his son Elah, which they had committed and caused Israel to commit, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger with their idols.
The rest of Elah’s deeds and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri became king in Tirzah for seven days. The people were encamped against Gath, which belonged to the Philistines.
The people in the camp heard it said, “Zimri has rebelled and has also killed the king.” That day in the camp, all Israel made Omri, the army commander, king over Israel.
Omri went up from Gath, with all Israel accompanying him, and they encamped against Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that Tirzah had been captured, he went into the inner chamber of the royal palace. They set the royal palace on fire over him, and he died.
This was because of the sins he had committed, doing what was evil before the Lord by following the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins he had caused Israel to commit.
The rest of Zimri’s deeds and the rebellion he carried out are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Then the people of Israel split into two factions. Half the people followed Tibni son of Ginath to make him king, and half followed Omri.
The people who followed Omri proved stronger than the people who followed Tibni. Tibni died, and Omri became king.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri became king over Israel and reigned for twelve years. He reigned in Tirzah for six years.
He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for a talent of silver and built on the hill. He named the city he built Samaria, after Shemer, the owner of the hill.
Omri did what was evil in the sight of the Lord and acted more wickedly than all the kings who were before him.
He followed all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins by which he caused Israel to sin, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger with their idols.
The rest of the acts of Omri, everything he did, and all his mighty deeds are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Omri rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria. His son Ahab became king after him.
Ahab son of Omri became king over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah. Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did more evil in the sight of the Lord than all who were before him.

As though following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat were a small thing in his eyes, he went and married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians. He went and served Baal and worshiped him.
He set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he built in Samaria.
Ahab served idols, and Ahab went further in serving them and provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

In his days Ahab rebuilt Jericho, the house of the curse. At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he completed it, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates, according to the word of the Lord that he spoke through Joshua son of Nun.

Elijah, who was from Tishbe, one of the settlers of Gilead, said to King Ahab, “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain during these years except when I say so.”
The word of the Lord came to him and said to him:
“Leave here, turn eastward, and hide by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.
You will drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
He went and did according to the word of the Lord. He went and stayed by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank water from the brook.
After some days the streams dried up, because no rain had fallen on the land.
The word of the Lord came to him, saying:
“Get up, go to Zarephath in Sidon, and stay there. I have commanded a widow there to feed you.”
He got up and went to Zarephath. He entered the gate of the town and saw a widow there gathering sticks. He called to her and said, “Bring me a little water in a container so I can drink.”
As she went to bring it to him, he called to her and said, “Bring me a piece of bread in your hand.”

She said, “As the Lord your God lives, I have nothing except a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a horn. I am gathering two sticks so that I can go and prepare it for myself and my son. We will eat it and then die.”
Elijah said to her, “Do not be afraid. Go and do as you have said. But first make a small cake of bread and bring it out to me. Afterward, make some for yourself and your son.”
“For this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not run out, and the horn of oil will not run dry, until the day the LORD sends rain on the face of the earth.’”
She went and did as Elijah had said, and she, he, and the members of his household ate during those days.
The jar of flour did not run out, and the horn of oil did not run dry, in accordance with the word of the LORD that he had spoken through Elijah.
After these events, the son of the woman who owned the house became sick. His illness became so severe that no breath remained in him.
She said to Elijah, “What do you have against me, prophet of God? Have you come to me to bring my sins to remembrance and to kill my son?”
Elijah said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him from her lap, carried him up to the upstairs room where he was staying, and laid him on his bed.
He called out to the LORD and said, “LORD God, have you brought disaster even on this widow with whom I am staying, by killing her son?”
He stretched himself over the boy three times and called to the Lord, saying, ‘Lord my God, let this boy’s life return to him.’
The LORD heard Elijah’s voice, and the boy’s soul returned to him, and he came to life.
Elijah took the boy, brought him down from the upstairs room into the house, and gave him to his mother. Elijah said to her, “Look, your son is alive!”
She said, “Now I know that you are a prophet of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is true.”
After many days, in the third year, the word of the LORD came to Elijah, saying, “Go, present yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain on the face of the earth.”
Elijah went to present himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
Ahab summoned Obadiah, who was in charge of his household. Obadiah feared the LORD greatly.
When Jezebel was killing the prophets of God, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them in a cave, fifty men at a time, and supplied them with bread and water.

Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land to all the springs of water and all the streams. Perhaps we can find grass and keep the horses and mules alive, so that we do not lose any of the livestock.”
They divided the route between them to travel through it. Ahab went alone along one route, and Obadiah went alone along another route.
While Obadiah was on the road, Elijah met him. Obadiah recognized him, fell facedown, and said to him, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
He said to him, “It is I.” Then he said to him, “Go, tell your master, ‘Elijah is here.’”
Obadiah said, “What sin have I committed, that you are handing your servant over to Ahab to have me killed?”

“As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my master has not sent someone to look for you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he made the kingdoms and nations swear that they had not found you.”
“And now you tell me, ‘Go, tell your master, “Elijah is here.”’”

“When I leave you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you away and take you somewhere I do not know. I will go and tell Ahab, but he will not find you, and he will kill me. Yet your servant has feared the LORD from his youth.”

Have I not told my lord what I did when Jezebel was killing the prophets of God? I took a hundred men from among the Lord’s prophets and hid them in a cave, fifty men at a time, and supplied them with bread and water.
“And now you tell me, ‘Go, tell your master, “Elijah is here,”’ and he will kill me!”
Elijah said, “As the LORD Almighty lives, whom I serve, I will surely present myself to him today.”
Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him, and Ahab came to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, he said to him, “Is it you, the one who troubles Israel?”
Elijah said to him, “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s household have, because you have abandoned the LORD’s commandments and followed Baal.”
“Now send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred and fifty prophets of the idols who eat at Jezebel’s table.”
Ahab sent word throughout all the Israelites and gathered the men at Mount Carmel.
Elijah approached all the people and said, ‘How long will you be divided between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; and if Baal is, follow him.’ But the people gave him no answer.
Elijah said, “I alone remain as a prophet of the LORD, but Baal’s prophets number four hundred and fifty men.”

“Let them give us two bulls. Let them choose one bull for themselves, cut it into pieces, and lay it on the wood, but put no fire under it. I will prepare one bull, cut it into pieces, and lay it on the wood, but put no fire under it.”
“Call on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of the LORD my God. The god who answers with fire is God.” All the people answered, “What you have said is good.”
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Choose one bull for yourselves and prepare it first, because there are many of you.”

They took the bull that had been given to them and prepared it. They kept calling on the name of Baal from morning until noon: “Baal, answer us!” But there was no sound and no one answered. They beat themselves at the altar they had made.

At noon Elijah mocked them and said, ‘Call out loudly, for he is a god! Perhaps he is thinking, or perhaps he is attending to some business, or perhaps he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and needs to wake up.’
They cried out loudly and cut themselves with swords and spears, as was their custom, until their blood poured out over them.

After noon had passed, they continued prophesying until the time when the offering was presented. But there was no sound, no one answered, and no one paid attention. Elijah said to the prophets of the idols, “Move aside now, and I too will prepare whole burnt offerings.” So they moved aside and went away.
Elijah said to all the people, “Come close to me.” All the people came close to him, and he repaired the LORD’s altar, which had been torn down.
Elijah took twelve stones, corresponding to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD had come, saying, “Your name shall be Israel.”
With the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. He made a trench around the altar enclosing an area large enough to sow two seahs of seed.
He arranged the wood, cut the bull into pieces, and laid it on top of the wood.

He said, “Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and the wood.” Then he said, “Do it a second time,” and they did it a second time. He said, “Do it a third time,” and they did it a third time.
The water ran around the altar, and they also filled the trench with water.

When the offering was presented, Elijah the prophet came forward and said, “LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your command.”
“Answer me, LORD, answer me, so that all these people may know that you, LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.”
The LORD’s fire fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench.
All the people saw it, fell on their faces, and said, “The LORD is God! The LORD is God!”
Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Do not let any of them escape!” They seized them, and Elijah brought them down to the Kishon stream and slaughtered them there.
Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a downpour.”
Ahab went up to eat and drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel, bent down to the ground, and put his face between his knees.
He said to his disciple, “Go up and look toward the sea.” He went up, looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He told him, “Go back seven times.”

The seventh time he said, “I looked, and there is a little cloud, like the palm of a hand, rising from the sea.” Elijah said to him, “Go up and tell Ahab, ‘Get into your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’”
While he was turning this way and that, the sky became covered with clouds and wind, and there was heavy rain. Ahab rode off and went to Jezreel.
The hand of the Lord was upon Elijah. He fastened his belt around his waist and ran ahead of Ahab until he entered Jezreel.
Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets of Baal and of [?] with the sword.
Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “May the gods do this to me, and more besides, if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them.”
Elijah was afraid and got up and went away to save his life. He came to Beersheba in Judah and left his disciple there.

He went a day’s journey into the wilderness and sat under a terebinth tree. He asked that he might die and said, ‘I have had enough now, Lord. Take my life from me, for I am no better than my ancestors.’
He lay down and fell sound asleep beneath the terebinth tree. Then an angel came up to him and said to him, “Get up and eat.”
He turned and saw at his head [?] bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He ate and drank, then lay down again.
The angel of the Lord returned a second time, came up to him, and said, “Get up, eat and drink, because the journey is too much for you.”
He got up, ate and drank, and with the strength from that food he traveled forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God.
He entered a cave there and spent the night there. The word of the Lord came to him and said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very zealous for the Lord, the mighty God, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altar, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life.”

He said to him, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord.” Then the Lord made a great and powerful wind that split mountains and shattered rocks before the Lord, but the Lord was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. After the fire came the sound of gentle speech.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. A voice came to him and said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very zealous for the Lord, the mighty God, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altar, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life.”
The Lord said to him, “Go back on your way to the wilderness of Damascus, and go and anoint Hazael to reign over Edom.
And anoint Jehu son of Nimshi to reign over Israel, and Elisha son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah, to be prophet in your place.
Jehu will kill whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, and Elisha will kill whoever escapes the sword of Jehu.
I will leave seven thousand in Israel: every knee that has not bowed to Baal and every mouth that has not kissed him.”
He went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat driving a team of oxen. Twelve teams were ahead of him, and he was one of the twelve. Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak over him.
He left the team of oxen and went after Elijah. He said to him, “Let me go and kiss my father and mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back, then, for what have I done to you?”

He turned back from following him, took the team of oxen, and slaughtered them. He cooked the meat using the oxen’s equipment, gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up and followed Elijah the prophet and served him.
Ben-hadad king of Edom gathered his entire army, with thirty-two kings who were with him, along with horses and chariots. He went up, laid siege to Samaria, and fought against it.
He sent messengers to Ahab king of Israel.
He said to him, “This is what Ben-hadad says: Your silver and gold are mine, and your beautiful wives and children are mine.”
The king of Israel answered, “As you say, my lord the king. I am yours, and so is everything I have.”
The messengers returned and said, “This is what Ben-hadad says: I sent word to you before that you must give me your silver and gold, your wives and your children.
Tomorrow at this time I will send my servants to you. They will search your houses and your servants’ houses, and they will take in their hands everything their eyes desire and bring it away.

The king of Israel summoned all the elders of the land and said to them, “Understand and see that this man is seeking trouble. He sent to me demanding my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, and I did not withhold them from him.”
All the elders and all the people said to him, “Do not listen to him or agree to his demands.”

He said to Ben-hadad’s messengers, “Tell my lord the king, ‘I will do everything you first sent word to your servant to do, but I cannot do this thing.’” The messengers went away and brought him the reply.
Ben-hadad sent word to him, saying, “May the gods do this to me, and more besides, if the dust of Samaria is enough to give each of the people with me a handful.”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘Let the one who straps on his armor not be regarded as the one who takes it off.’”
When he heard this message, he and the kings were drinking in the shelters. He said to his servants, “Lay siege to the city.”

Then a prophet approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Do you see this whole great army? Look, I am handing it over to you today, and you will know that I am the Lord.’”
Ahab said, “Through whom?” He told him, “Through the young men and the officials of the province.” He asked him, “Who should begin the battle?” He answered, “You.”
He counted the young men and the officials of the province, and there were 232. After them he counted all the people, all the Israelites: seven thousand.
They went out at noon, while Ben-hadad was drinking aged wine in the shelters with the thirty-two kings who had come to help him.
The young men and the officials of the province went out first. Ben-hadad sent men out, and they reported to him, “Look, men have come out of Samaria.”
He said, “If they have come out for peace, capture them alive; and if they have come out for battle, capture them alive.”
These went out of the city: the young men and the officials of the province, with the army behind them.
Each man killed his opponent. Edom fled, and Israel pursued them. Ben-hadad king of Edom escaped with chariots and horsemen.
The king of Israel went out and destroyed the horses and chariots, and inflicted a very great defeat on Edom.

Then a prophet of God approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “Go, strengthen yourself, and consider carefully what you must do, because at the turn of the year the king of Edom will come up against you.”
The servants of the king of Edom said to him, “Their god is a god of the mountains. That is why he defeated us. But let us fight them on the plain, and we will surely defeat them.
Do this: remove each of the kings from his position and appoint commanders in their place.
And muster an army equal to the army you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. Let us fight them on the plain, and we will surely be stronger than they are.” He listened to them and did so.
At the turn of the year, Ben-hadad mustered Edom and went up to Aphek to fight Israel.
The Israelites were mustered and drawn up in formation. They stood facing them like two flocks of young goats, while the Edomites filled the land.

A prophet of God approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Because the Edomites have said that the Lord is a god of the mountains and not a god of the valleys, I will hand this whole great army over to you, and you will know that I am the Lord.’”
They camped opposite one another for seven days. On the seventh day they joined battle, and the Israelites killed a hundred thousand Edomite foot soldiers in a single day.
The survivors fled to the city of Aphek, and the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of the remaining men. Ben-hadad fled and went into the city, into an inner room.

His servants approached him and said, “Look, we have heard that the kings of Israel are kind kings. Let us tie sackcloth around our heads and ropes around our waists, and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare our lives.”

They tied sackcloth around their heads and ropes around their waists, came to the king of Israel, and said to him, “Your servant Ben-hadad says, ‘Let me live.’” He said, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.”

Now Ben-hadad was a man who looked for omens. The men whispered and hurried to draw this statement from him, saying, “Your brother Ben-hadad!” He said, “Go and bring him.” Ben-hadad came out to him, and he seated him beside himself in the chariot.

He said to him, “I will restore to you the towns my father took from your father, and I will establish a marketplace for you in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” “And I will send you away under a treaty.” So he made a treaty with him and sent him away.
One of the company of prophets said to his companion by the word of the Lord, “Strike me.” But the man refused to strike him.
He said to him, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of the Lord your God, as soon as you leave me, a lion will kill you.” He left him, and a lion found him and killed him.
He found another man and said to him, “Strike me.” That man struck him and wounded him.
The prophet went and stood beside the road before the king, covering his face with ashes.

As the king passed by, he cried out before the king and said, “Your servant went into the battle, and a man turned aside and brought me a man. He said to me, ‘Guard this man. If he goes missing, your life will be for his life, or you must pay a talent of silver.’
While your servant was turning this way and that, the man disappeared.” The king of Israel said to him, “That is your sentence; you have pronounced it yourself.”
He hurried and removed the ashes from his face, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets.
He said to him, “This is what the Lord says: Because you released the man doomed to destruction from [?], your life will be for his life, and your people for his people.”
The king of Israel went home, distressed and angry, and entered Samaria.
After these events, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.

Ahab said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard so that I can make it a vegetable garden, since it is close beside my house. I will give you a better vineyard in exchange, or, if you prefer, I will pay you its value in silver.”
Naboth said to Ahab, “The Lord forbid that I should give you my ancestors’ inheritance!”

Ahab went home distressed and angry because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had said to him: “I will not give you my ancestors’ inheritance.” He lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and would not eat.
His wife Jezebel came to him and said, “Why are you so distressed that you do not want to eat?”

He said to her, “Because I said to Naboth the Jezreelite, ‘Give me your vineyard for silver, or, if you wish, I will give you a better vineyard in exchange.’ But he said to me, ‘I will not give you my vineyard.’”
His wife Jezebel said to him, “Are you capable of being king over Israel? Get up, eat, and cheer up. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
She wrote a letter in Ahab’s name, sealed it with his signet ring, and sent the letter to the elders and nobles who lived in the town with Naboth.
She wrote in the letter, “Proclaim a fast and seat Naboth at the head of the people.
Bring two wicked men and seat them opposite him. Let them testify against him and say, ‘Naboth has reviled God and the king.’ Then take him out and stone him to death.”
The men of his town—the elders and nobles who lived in the town with Naboth—did as Jezebel had instructed them, as it was written in the letter she had sent them.
They proclaimed a fast and seated Naboth at the head of the people.

They brought two wicked men and seated them opposite him. Those men testified against Naboth, saying, “Naboth has reviled God and the king.” They took him outside the town and stoned him with stones, and he died.
They sent word to Jezebel that Naboth had been stoned and had died.

When Jezebel heard that Naboth had died, she said to Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who refused to sell it to you for money, because Naboth is dead and is no longer alive.”
When Ahab heard that Naboth had died, he got up to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite to take possession of it.
The word of the LORD came to Elijah from Tishbe, saying:
“Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. He is there in the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, where he has gone down to take possession of it.”

Say to him, ‘This is what the Lord says: You have killed, and now you have taken possession! This is what the Lord says: In the place where dogs licked Naboth’s blood, dogs will also lick your own blood.’
Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He replied, “I have found you, because you have acted arrogantly in doing evil before the LORD.
“Look, I am bringing disaster upon you. I will sweep away your descendants and destroy every male belonging to Ahab who urinates against a wall, both those bound and those free in Israel.
I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have provoked anger and caused Israel to sin.
The LORD also said concerning Jezebel, ‘Dogs will eat Jezebel on the estate at Jezreel.’
Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city, dogs will eat; and anyone belonging to him who dies in the open country, the birds of the sky will eat.”
Indeed, there was no one like Ahab, who set his mind on doing evil before the LORD, urged on by his wife Jezebel.
He became utterly defiled and followed idols, as the Amorites had done, whom the Lord destroyed before the Israelites.
When Ahab heard this word, he tore his clothes, covered his body with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked barefoot.
The word of the LORD came to Elijah from Tishbe, saying:

“Have you seen how Ahab has felt shame before me? Because he has felt shame before me, I will not bring the disaster during his lifetime. During his son’s lifetime I will bring the disaster upon his house.”
They remained for three years without war between Edom and Israel.
In the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to Ahab king of Israel.
The king of Israel said to his servants, “You know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us. How long will we remain quiet instead of taking it from the king of Edom?”
He said to Jehoshaphat, ‘Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?’ Jehoshaphat said, ‘I will go as you do; my people are like your people, and my horses are like your horses.’
Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire today for the word of the LORD.”

The king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and said to them, “Should I go to Ramoth-gilead to fight, or should I stay here?” They said to him, “Go up! The LORD will deliver them into your hands, O king.”
Jehoshaphat said, “Is there no prophet of God here whom we can consult?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we can inquire for the word of the LORD, but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good about me, only evil. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king should not speak that way.”
The king of Israel called an official and said to him, “Quickly bring Micaiah son of Imlah.”
The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting, each on his throne, wearing embroidered robes, at the entrance to the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying before them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns for himself and said, “This is what the LORD says: With these you will gore the Edomites until you destroy them.”
All the prophets were prophesying the same thing, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead! You will be victorious, and the LORD will deliver them into your hands, O king.”

The messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, “Look, the false prophets have unanimously spoken favorably about the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably too.”
Micaiah said, “As the Lord lives, I will say only what the Lord tells me.”
He came to the king, and the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall we refrain?” He said to him, “Go up and win! The Lord will hand them over to you, O king.”
The king said to him, “How many times must I put you under oath to tell me nothing but the truth in the name of the Lord?”
Micaiah said, “I saw Israel scattered over the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. The Lord said, ‘These have no master. Let each return home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he prophesies nothing good about me, but only evil?”
Micaiah said, ‘Therefore hear the word of the Lord: I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing above him, on his right and on his left.’
The Lord said, “Who will entice Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” One said one thing, and another said another.
A spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, “I will entice him.” The Lord said to him, “How?”
He said, “I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” He said to him, “You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go out and do so.”
“Now look, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the Lord has pronounced disaster against you.”
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said to him, “Which way did the spirit of the Lord pass from me to speak through you?”
Micaiah said to him, “You will see on the day when you go into an inner room to hide.”
The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah and hand him over to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king’s son.
Tell them, ‘This is what the king says: Put this man in prison. Feed him only enough bread to keep him alive, and give him only enough water to keep him alive, until I return safely.’”
Micaiah said, “If you return safely, the Lord has not spoken through me.” And he said, “Listen, all you peoples!”
The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and enter the battle, but you wear your robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself and entered the battle.
The king of Edom commanded his thirty-two chariot commanders, saying, “Do not fight anyone, small or great, but only the king of Israel.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought he was the king of Israel and turned toward him to fight him. Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned away from him.

One man shot his bow ahead of him without knowing whom he would hit, and struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. The king said to his charioteer, “Turn around and take me out of the camp, for I am mortally wounded.”
The battle grew fierce that day, and the king remained standing in his chariot facing Edom. He died in the evening, and the blood from his wound flowed into the bottom of his chariot.
At sunset a herald called out in the camp, saying, “Go, each man to his own city and each to his own land!”
The king died and was brought to Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.
They washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria and washed his armor, and the dogs licked up his blood, according to the word that the Lord had spoken.
The rest of Ahab’s deeds, everything he did, the ivory house he built, and all the towns he built are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Ahab rested with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king after him.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother’s name was Arubah daughter of Shilhi.
He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn aside from them. He did what was right in the sight of the Lord.
However, he did not remove the high places, and the people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense at the high places.
Jehoshaphat made peace with the kings of Israel.
The rest of Jehoshaphat’s deeds, all the mighty acts he performed, and the battles he fought are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
He removed from the land the rest of the prostitution that had remained in the days of his father Asa.
There was no reigning king in Edom.
Jehoshaphat built ships for Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but he did not go, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships.” But Jehoshaphat was unwilling.
Jehoshaphat rested with his ancestors and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David his ancestor. His son Jehoram became king after him.
Ahaziah son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. He reigned over Israel for two years.
He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord. He followed the ways of his father, the ways of his mother, and the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.
He served Baal and worshiped him, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done.
